title: What is known about 1RB0RA_0RC0LB_1LD1RF_1LE1RA_1RD1RB_1LA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RA_0RC0LB_1LD1RF_1LE1RA_1RD1RB_1LA---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is a regular round structure (the total length of the blocks doubles each round, a round takes about four times as long as the one before); one round step is proved in Lean for all counts, the rounds are observed, not proved, and nothing found so far says whether the halting transition (F reading 1) can ever fire.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The block cycle, for all counts
claims.text: With the head in C at the right end of b^(n+1) 1 a^(m+1) 1 c 1 a^(k+1) 0000 c (a = 11010, b = 10000, c = 10), the machine turns the last b into an a and lengthens the last run of a by one in 50k + 50m + 287 steps, without reading the tape left of the block: the bouncer's elementary move.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 44,483 cells have been visited and 14,559 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.062). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.487).

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>12</sup> steps
claims.text: The cycle accelerator of the shared tools (bbtools.cycles, blocks of 5 cells; every jump applies a one-cycle rule it proved symbolically) runs the machine 1012 steps (13 rounds and part of the 14th) without a halt.

claims.title: No closed tape language from windows up to 7
claims.text: bbtools.ctl with windows of K = 2 to 6 cells closes but allows F to read a 1 (6 to 192 abstract halting configurations); with K = 7 it finds no closed set within its round limit. The n-gram CPS decider (widths 3 to 7, with history and LRU augmentations) also fails.

claims.title: Rounds: the new block is the sum of the old ones
claims.text: At the start of each round the tape is a small gadget at the left end, then blocks b^n1 c 00 b^n2 c 00 ... b^nk. During the round the bouncer works from the right, turning each block into a's one b per pair of sweeps while a tail of a's at the right end grows by one per b; at the end of the round a pass from the left turns everything back into b's and the tail becomes a new block. So the new block is (up to a few cells) the sum of all the blocks, the total doubles: 3, 21, 61, 152, 341, 720, 1491, 3038, 6138, 12339, 24743, 49564, 99212. In some rounds (2·106, 2.6·109 steps) the new block absorbs the previous largest one instead of standing next to it. Observed in the first 6.5·1011 steps, not proved.

claims.title: Why the left side grows like a logarithm
claims.text: The head reaches the far left only once per round, where the gadget (a small counter) gains about two cells; rounds take four times longer each, so the left reach grows like log<sub>4</sub> of the step count. The right side grows by 5 cells every two sweeps: a bouncer, square-root growth.

claims.title: A round map for the whole block list, checked against the direct run
claims.text: Sample the run whenever the head is in state B reading 0 with only 0s to its left (about once or twice a round). The tape is cut into runs of repeated words and short literals; the next sample is computed from simulations in which every long run is short, one run at a time is lengthened, and two further instances check that the new counts are affine in the old ones. Along the direct run from blank tape to 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps (18 samples) this map predicts all 17 next samples exactly. An extrapolation checked by computation, not a proof.

claims.title: 40 more samples past the direct run, no halt
claims.text: Iterated from the last sample of the direct run: 40 samples without a halt; the list then has about 50 blocks and the largest holds a count of 69 bits (the direct run reaches 14 bits). The blocks keep the shape (10100)^n 1 000 and roughly double. The run was stopped by a time limit after round 40, not by an event of the machine; the classes change every round (a block is added), so each round costs new simulations. An earlier run with a fixed threshold stopped after 33 samples at a class whose simulations disagreed, when two blocks of about 20 words stood next to the left-end gadget; with the threshold raised for such rounds the iteration passes that point.

claims.title: Does it halt?
claims.text: Not known. The machine halts only when F reads a 1; F is entered (from C reading a 1) about 2% of all steps and in the first 2·108 steps (4,004,892 visits) it always had 0101 to its left. Whether a round can ever end in a configuration where it reads a 1 depends on the left-end gadget and on how blocks merge, which are not understood yet.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 44,483 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.eyebrow: What the tape is made of
sections.heading: Blocks of 10000 and 11010
html: Read in words of five cells, the tape is very regular. Writing a = 11010, b = 10000 and c = 10, the tape at the start of the round at step 10,278,686,777 is
a short gadget at the left end, then a list of blocks b^n separated by c 00, and the head (in state C) at the right end. Everything the machine does is a slow transformation of this list.

sections.heading: Two sweeps turn one b into an a
html: Inside a round the head bounces between the right end and the block it is working on. Each pair of sweeps turns the last b of that block into an a and adds one a to a tail at the right end, five cells further out. In Lean (sweep, all counts):
b^(n+1) 1 a^(m+1) 1 c 1 a^(k+1) 0000 c C>  →  b^n 1 a^(m+2) 1 c 1 a^(k+2) 0000 c C>   (50k + 50m + 287 steps)
When a block is used up the head starts on the next one to the left, and the tail keeps growing: by the end of the round it has gained one a for every b on the tape.

sections.eyebrow: The rule from one round to the next
sections.heading: Each new block is the sum of the old ones
html: When all blocks are a's, the head runs to the left end, steps the gadget there, and a pass back turns the a's into b's again; the tail becomes a new block. The new block is, up to a few cells, the total of all the blocks before it, so the total doubles every round (totals 3, 21, 61, 152, 341, 720, 1491, 3038, 6138, 12339, 24743, 49564, 99212 in the first 6.5·1011 steps). Since each round sweeps a tape twice as long twice as many times, it takes about four times as long as the last one.

A worked example: the round starting at step 2,568,368,685 has blocks 11, 4, 12, 26, 49, 287, 387, 780, 1554, 9305 (sum 12,415), and the next round starts with a new block of exactly 12,415. Now and then (the rounds at 2·106 and 2.6·109 steps) the new block swallows the largest old block instead, which is why 9305 is about three times 3096.

sections.heading: Only F reading a 1 stops it
html: The only halting transition is F on a 1. F is entered after C reads a 1, about once every 50 steps, and so far always with 0101 to its left and a 0 under the head. The regular part of a round (the block cycle above) never brings F onto a 1; a halt would have to come from the irregular moments: the turn at the left end, and the merging of blocks. These are not understood yet, so the question stays open; there is no probabilistic picture either way.

sections.heading: A round map for the whole block list
html: A direct run needs about four times as many steps for each new round, so it stops near round 13. To go further, the tape at the left-end turn is cut into runs of repeated words, and the next turn is computed from small instances: every long run is made short, then lengthened one at a time, and the new counts are fitted as affine functions of the old ones, with two more instances as a check.

This map predicts all 17 of the left-end turns of the direct run to 3·109 steps exactly. Iterated beyond it, 40 more turns pass without a halt; by then the list has about 50 blocks and the largest count has 69 bits. The computation was stopped by a time limit, not by anything the machine did.
This is an observed law, not a proved one, and 40 turns say little about a machine whose irregular moments (the gadget at the left end, blocks merging) are not understood. The question stays open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.062). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.487).
After 109 steps the tape spans 44,483 cells (34 left of the start, 29,274 right), with a density of 1s of 0.327.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A stack of blocks of b = 10000 that a bouncer turns, one cell-block per two sweeps, into a = 11010 and back; each round adds a new block as long as all the others together, so the total doubles every round.
